title: The Phone Careem's Founders Took Turns Sleeping Beside
dek: In 2012 two McKinsey consultants in Dubai started a car-booking service with $100,000, twenty drivers and one very loud phone.

story.event: Leaving McKinsey to start a corporate car-booking service in Dubai
story.summary: After surviving a brain bleed at 29, McKinsey consultant Magnus Olsson quit to build something 'big and meaningful' with his colleague Mudassir Sheikha; a senior partner suggested ground transport, and with $100,000 of their own money they launched Careem in Dubai in July 2012 as a car-booking service for companies. They interviewed their first twenty drivers in a car park and took turns sleeping beside the phone that received bookings; in September 2013 they raised $1.7 million led by STC Ventures, and Careem later became a ride-hailing app that Uber bought in 2020.
paragraphs: At 29, Magnus Olsson, a Swedish consultant with McKinsey in the Middle East, had a bleed in his brain and nearly died; several operations cured him. He later said it made him think hard about what he wanted from life: "I cannot live my life just surviving." He quit, and asked a colleague in McKinsey's Dubai office, Mudassir Sheikha, who had worked for technology start-ups before consulting, to help him find something big and meaningful to build.

They called the search Project Bamboo and listed problems they had met in the region. They looked at health care, education and fish farms, which Olsson said they dropped because they would smell of fish. When Sheikha told a McKinsey senior partner, Tarek Elmasry, he was taking time off to think, Elmasry asked: what about ground transport? As travelling consultants they knew the passenger's side, booking a driver in Cairo or Doha and hoping he would arrive on time and find the way. Otherwise, Olsson admitted, "We knew nothing about transportation." Before any business plan, they wrote down their values and purpose, and chose a name, Careem, Arabic for generous.

They started, Sheikha recalled, with $100,000, and after paying for an office, a deposit to accept credit cards and licences, "we were down $60,000 to $70,000." Careem opened in Dubai in July 2012 as a service for companies booking cars for their staff. The founders interviewed their first twenty drivers one by one in a car park in International City; Olsson ran English and Arabic tests and asked each candidate how to reach fifteen difficult locations.

The system was rough. A booking on the website sent an email to a phone with a very loud ringtone. Customers booked at night, so the founders took turns sleeping with it, then rang down the list of drivers to find one who was free. Often, Olsson said, they ended up at the wrong house. By September 2013 Careem said it had more than 1,000 cars in its network across Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Doha and Riyadh, and it raised its first outside money: $1.7 million, led by STC Ventures.
It later became a ride-hailing app, and in 2020 Uber completed its purchase of the company for about $3.1 billion.

quote.text: And he who lives a hundred years, not seeing beginning and end, a life of one day is better if a man sees beginning and end.
quote.source_title: Dhammapada, a Collection of Verses, tr. F. Max Müller, Project Gutenberg eBook #2017
quote.connection: The verse weighs one day lived seeing beginning and end above a hundred years lived without that sight. Olsson met his own ending early, at 29; what followed was not a slower life but a clearer one, and Careem's purpose was written down before its business plan.

reflection: Most people never get a warning like Olsson's, and nobody should want one. But the question it forced on him is available on an ordinary morning: what is this work for, and would you still choose it if the time were shorter than you think? He and Sheikha answered that in writing before they answered anything else.

The rest was unglamorous: a car park, a list of twenty phone numbers, a phone that rang at night. Writing the purpose down did not make those nights easier, but it told them why the phone was worth answering. If your own nights have been long lately, your body's view of that counts too.
invitation: Write one sentence saying what your work is for, in words a colleague would understand. If it will not come, leave the line blank and try again tomorrow.

cross_checks.claim: Careem was founded in Dubai in 2012 by former McKinsey consultants Magnus Olsson and Mudassir Sheikha
It began as a car-booking service for corporate customers
Olsson's near-fatal brain bleed led him to leave McKinsey and look for something meaningful to build
The idea of ground transport came from a former colleague
In September 2013 Careem raised $1.7 million in a round led by STC Ventures
Uber completed its acquisition of Careem in 2020 for about $3 billion

research_notes: Kept distinct from the Swvl and Souq editions: this is Careem's own founding and first year, not a later restructuring. Start-up money: Sheikha told McKinsey they began with $100,000 and that after paying for an office, a credit-card acceptance deposit and licensing 'we were down $60,000 to $70,000'; it is unclear whether that is the amount spent or the amount left, so the story quotes his words rather than interpreting them. Founding date: Careem's September 2013 press release says it was established in July 2012; other sources say only 2012. The figure of more than 1,000 cars 'across its network' in four cities in 2013 is Careem's own claim in that release and is attributed as such. Acquisition price: McKinsey and Entrepreneur Middle East say $3 billion, Monocle $3.1 billion; Uber's purchase was agreed in 2019 and completed in 2020; the story says 'about $3.1 billion' in 2020. Funding is 'bootstrapped' for the episode: the first year ran on the founders' $100,000 (and, per the Talks at Google transcript, their savings), before the first outside round in September 2013. The McKinsey interview is cited from McKinsey's Brazil site because mckinsey.com blocks automated requests; it is the same text. The Talks at Google transcript is machine-generated (it renders the company's name as 'Kareem'), so it is used only for facts confirmed elsewhere and no quotation is taken from it. Ramadan: some accounts say Careem launched during Ramadan; no loadable source confirmed it, so it is left out. Who conducted the driver interviews: Olsson says 'we' interviewed the twenty captains and that he conducted the English and Arabic tests; the story follows that. The Dhammapada verse concerns insight into arising and passing away; it is applied to Olsson's brush with death by analogy.
